cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 34-year-old woman has six months of fatigue and heavy periods. Her results are hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL (12.0–15.5) · mean corpuscular volume 72 fL (80–100) · ferritin 6 ng/mL (15–200) · total iron-binding capacity 465 µg/dL (250–400). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Iron deficiency anemia

Correct. Microcytic with a LOW ferritin and a HIGH iron-binding capacity — the marrow is short of iron and the body has increased its carrying capacity to hunt for more. In a menstruating woman this is the commonest anemia there is, and it still obliges you to think about occult blood loss.
Anemia of chronic disease
This gives a low iron too, but ferritin is an acute phase reactant and rises; the binding capacity FALLS rather than rises. Both markers here point the other way.
Beta thalassemia trait
Also microcytic, but iron studies are normal — ferritin would not be 6. The red cell count also tends to be preserved or high, which is what separates it.
Vitamin B12 deficiency
That is macrocytic, with a volume above 100 rather than 72. Wrong side of the algorithm entirely.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, iron studies

cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 68-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis has mild fatigue. His results are hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · mean corpuscular volume 84 fL (80–100) · ferritin 410 ng/mL (15–200) · total iron-binding capacity 198 µg/dL (250–400). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Anemia of chronic disease

Correct. Ferritin HIGH and binding capacity LOW is the mirror image of iron deficiency: iron exists but inflammation sequesters it, and ferritin rises as an acute phase reactant. The volume sits normocytic or mildly microcytic.
Iron deficiency anemia
Would show the opposite pair — ferritin low, binding capacity high. A ferritin of 410 effectively excludes it.
Sideroblastic anemia
Iron is high here too, but this is far rarer and the smear shows ringed sideroblasts on iron staining rather than an inflammatory picture.
Folate deficiency
Macrocytic, and it does not move ferritin or binding capacity in this pattern.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, iron studies

cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 24-year-old man of Mediterranean descent is anemic on a routine panel and feels well. His results are hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · mean corpuscular volume 68 fL (80–100) · red blood cell count 6.1 million/µL (4.5–5.9) · ferritin 142 ng/mL (15–200). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Beta thalassemia trait
Correct. Markedly microcytic with NORMAL iron stores and a red cell count that is high rather than low — the marrow makes plenty of small cells. Iron deficiency cannot produce that combination.
Iron deficiency anemia
Ferritin is normal at 142, and the red cell count would be low rather than 6.1 million. Both findings argue against it.
Anemia of chronic disease
There is no inflammatory context, the anemia is mild, and the degree of microcytosis is far greater than this usually produces.
Lead poisoning
Also microcytic with normal iron, but the smear shows basophilic stippling and there would be an exposure history.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, microcytic causes

cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 71-year-old man has fatigue and pins and needles in both feet. His results are hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · mean corpuscular volume 118 fL (80–100) · vitamin B12 94 pg/mL (200–900) · smear macroovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (—). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Folate deficiency
Produces an identical smear, but the B12 level here is the discriminator — and folate deficiency does not cause the neurological findings.
Alcoholic liver disease
A common non-megaloblastic macrocytosis, but it does NOT produce macroovalocytes or hypersegmented neutrophils. Their presence points at impaired DNA synthesis.
Myelodysplastic syndrome
Can be macrocytic, but usually with cytopenias in more than one line and dysplastic changes rather than a pure megaloblastic picture.
Vitamin B12 deficiency

Correct. Macrocytic with a low B12, and the smear gives the megaloblastic signature — macroovalocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils. The neuropathy is what distinguishes it from folate deficiency clinically.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, macrocytic causes

cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 52-year-old man who drinks heavily is anemic. His results are hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · mean corpuscular volume 106 fL (80–100) · vitamin B12 and folate both normal (—) · smear round macrocytes, no hypersegmentation (—). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Vitamin B12 deficiency
Excluded by a normal B12, and the smear lacks the megaloblastic changes it would produce.
Non-megaloblastic macrocytosis of liver disease and alcohol

Correct. Macrocytic with normal B12 and folate and, decisively, NO macroovalocytes or hypersegmented neutrophils. Without those the problem is not DNA synthesis, and alcohol and liver disease are the usual explanation.
Folate deficiency
Folate is normal, and it would give the same hypersegmented picture that is absent here.
Hereditary spherocytosis
That raises the mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration and shows spherocytes; it does not produce macrocytosis.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, macrocytic causes

cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 29-year-old woman is admitted after a road traffic collision with a pelvic fracture. Two days later her results are hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL (12.0–15.5) · mean corpuscular volume 89 fL (80–100) · reticulocyte count 6.8% (0.5–2.5) · ferritin 165 ng/mL (15–200). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Iron deficiency anemia
Takes weeks to develop and would be microcytic with a low ferritin. Neither is present two days after the injury.
Acute blood loss anemia

Correct. Normocytic with a HIGH reticulocyte count — the marrow is responding normally to a sudden loss, and the cells it makes are of normal size. Stores are still adequate, which is why ferritin is untouched this early.
Aplastic anemia
The marrow would be failing, so the reticulocyte count would be LOW rather than 6.8%, and other cell lines would fall too.
Anemia of chronic disease
Develops over weeks of inflammation and is hypo-proliferative — the reticulocyte response would be blunted, not brisk.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, normocytic branch

cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 26-year-old woman has jaundice and dark urine. Her results are hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL (12.0–15.5) · reticulocyte count 9.2% (0.5–2.5) · unconjugated bilirubin 4.1 mg/dL (0.2–0.8) · haptoglobin undetectable (30–200 mg/dL). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute blood loss anemia
Also raises reticulocytes, but blood leaving the body does not release hemoglobin into plasma, so haptoglobin and bilirubin stay normal.
Hemolytic anemia

Correct. A high reticulocyte count with a raised UNCONJUGATED bilirubin and an undetectable haptoglobin is the hemolysis triad — cells are being destroyed, free hemoglobin is mopping up the haptoglobin, and the marrow is compensating hard.
Gilbert syndrome
Raises unconjugated bilirubin, but causes no anemia, no reticulocytosis and no haptoglobin consumption.
Aplastic anemia
The reticulocyte count would be low and there would be no hyperbilirubinemia; the marrow is not producing.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, hemolysis

cbc.io: e — Discuss the clinical significance of abnormalities in red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
cbc.q: A 33-year-old man has fatigue, bruising and recurrent infections. His results are hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · white blood cell count 1,900/µL (4,500–11,000) · platelets 24,000/µL (150,000–400,000) · reticulocyte count 0.2% (0.5–2.5). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
Drops platelets alone. Hemoglobin and white cells would be normal, and they are not.
Aplastic anemia

Correct. All three lines are down and the reticulocyte count is LOW — the marrow is not producing anything. That combination of pancytopenia with an absent reticulocyte response is what defines marrow failure.
Hemolytic anemia
Would drive reticulocytes UP, and does not by itself cause leukopenia or thrombocytopenia.
Iron deficiency anemia
Affects the red line only, is microcytic, and if anything raises the platelet count rather than lowering it.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, pancytopenia

cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 4-year-old living in old housing has irritability and abdominal pain. Her results are hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL (11.5–15.5) · mean corpuscular volume 70 fL (80–100) · ferritin 88 ng/mL (15–200) · smear coarse basophilic stippling (—). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Iron deficiency anemia
The commonest microcytic anemia at this age, but ferritin is normal at 88 and it does not produce stippling.
Beta thalassemia trait
Microcytic with normal iron as well, and it is the differential here — but stippling points to lead, and thalassemia usually preserves the red cell count.
Anemia of chronic disease
There is no inflammatory illness, and it does not cause stippling.
Lead poisoning
Correct. Microcytic with NORMAL iron stores, and the smear finding settles it — basophilic stippling is ribosomal RNA scattered evenly through the cytoplasm, and the classic association is lead.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, red cell inclusions

cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 22-year-old man has anemia and splenomegaly. His results are hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · mean corpuscular volume 82 fL (80–100) · mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration 38 g/dL (32–36) · smear round cells lacking central pallor (—). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Iron deficiency anemia
Moves the concentration DOWN, not up, and produces hypochromic cells with widened central pallor — the opposite appearance.
Sickle cell disease
The smear would show thin crescents forming under low oxygen tension, not uniformly round cells.
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
Can also produce spherocytes, but they are acquired and the direct antiglobulin test is positive; the hereditary form runs in families.
Hereditary spherocytosis

Correct. A RAISED mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration is the automated flag for it, and the smear matches — perfectly round cells that have lost their central pallor. Few things push that index above the range.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration

cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 30-year-old man had a splenectomy after trauma five years ago. His routine smear shows single dark purple nuclear fragments in red cells present (absent) · target cells present (absent) · hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL (13.5–17.5). What is the most likely cause?
opts: Iron deficiency has produced the inclusions
Iron deficiency gives hypochromic microcytic cells; it does not leave nuclear remnants behind, and the hemoglobin here is normal.
He has lead poisoning
Lead gives basophilic stippling — fine blue dots spread evenly through the cytoplasm — not a single discrete nuclear fragment.
He has no spleen to remove the inclusions

Correct. Those fragments are Howell-Jolly bodies, and the spleen normally plucks them out — so finding them means absent or non-functioning splenic tissue. Target cells appear after splenectomy too, from redundant membrane.
He has glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
That shows Heinz bodies, which are denatured hemoglobin at the cell periphery and need a supravital stain to see at all.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, Howell-Jolly bodies

cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 19-year-old man develops anemia days after starting an oxidant drug. His results are hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · reticulocyte count 7.1% (0.5–2.5) · supravital stain inclusions at the cell periphery (—) · smear bite cells (—). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hereditary spherocytosis
Gives round cells without central pallor and a raised hemoglobin concentration index, and it is not triggered by oxidant drugs.
Immune hemolytic anemia
Would be confirmed by a positive direct antiglobulin test and does not need a supravital stain to show inclusions.
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

Correct. Heinz bodies are denatured hemoglobin sitting at the edge of the cell and are invisible without a supravital stain; the spleen bites them out, leaving bite cells. An oxidant trigger completes the picture.
Lead poisoning
Basophilic stippling is visible on the ordinary stain and is spread through the cytoplasm, not at the periphery.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, Heinz bodies

cbc.io: e — Discuss the clinical significance of abnormalities in red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
cbc.q: A 41-year-old woman has a fever and a productive cough. Her results are white blood cell count 19,400/µL (4,500–11,000) · neutrophils 84% (54–62) · bands 11% (0–5) · lymphocytes 9% (24–44). What is the most likely cause?
opts: A viral infection
Would raise LYMPHOCYTES rather than neutrophils, and lymphocytes here are suppressed at 9%.
A parasitic infestation
Raises eosinophils, which are not elevated in this differential.
A bacterial infection
Correct. Neutrophils dominate and bands are raised — a left shift, meaning the marrow is releasing immature neutrophils faster than it can mature them. That pairing is the bacterial signature.
An allergic reaction
Also an eosinophil response, and it would not produce a band count of 11%.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, neutrophils and left shift

cbc.io: e — Discuss the clinical significance of abnormalities in red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
cbc.q: A 9-year-old has a week of fever, sore throat and fatigue. His results are white blood cell count 14,800/µL (4,500–11,000) · lymphocytes 62% (24–44) · neutrophils 28% (54–62) · smear atypical lymphocytes (—). What is the most likely cause?
opts: A bacterial infection
Would push neutrophils up with a left shift; here neutrophils are the suppressed line.
A viral infection
Correct. A lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis with atypical lymphocytes on the smear is the viral pattern, and in this age group with pharyngitis it points hard at infectious mononucleosis.
An allergic reaction
Drives eosinophils, and produces neither lymphocytosis nor atypical forms.
A bone marrow failure syndrome
The total white count is raised rather than reduced, so production is not the problem.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, lymphocytes

cbc.io: e — Discuss the clinical significance of abnormalities in red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
cbc.q: A 27-year-old man recently back from travel has itching and a rash. His results are white blood cell count 12,100/µL (4,500–11,000) · eosinophils 18% (1–3) · neutrophils 48% (54–62) · hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL (13.5–17.5). What is the most likely cause?
opts: A parasitic infestation or an allergic process
Correct. Eosinophils are the line raised by parasites, allergy and — less often — malignancy. At 18% against a range of 1 to 3, the eosinophil is the whole finding here.
A bacterial infection
Neutrophils would lead and would be raised rather than mildly low.
A viral infection
Lymphocytes carry the viral response; eosinophils are not the viral line.
Corticosteroid therapy
Steroids raise neutrophils by demargination and actually SUPPRESS eosinophils.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, eosinophils

cbc.io: d — Calculate absolute white blood cell counts
cbc.q: A patient on chemotherapy is reviewed before the next cycle. His results are white blood cell count 1,200/µL (4,500–11,000) · neutrophils 22% (54–62) · bands 6% (0–5). Calculate the absolute neutrophil count and grade it.
opts: 336 per microlitre — severe neutropenia
Correct. Bands count WITH the neutrophils: 1,200 × (22 + 6) ÷ 100 = 336. Below 500 is severe, which is the threshold that changes precautions and antibiotic decisions.
264 per microlitre — severe neutropenia
This leaves the bands out. They are immature neutrophils and belong in the numerator — that omission is the classic error.
336 per microlitre — moderate neutropenia
The arithmetic is right but the grade is not: moderate is 500 to under 1,000, and 336 is below 500.
1,200 per microlitre — mild neutropenia
That is the total white count, not the neutrophil count. A percentage means nothing until it is applied to the total.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, absolute neutrophil count

cbc.io: e — Discuss the clinical significance of abnormalities in red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
cbc.q: A 28-year-old woman has petechiae and gum bleeding after a viral illness. She is otherwise well. Her results are platelets 18,000/µL (150,000–400,000) · hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL (12.0–15.5) · white blood cell count 7,100/µL (4,500–11,000) · smear no schistocytes (—). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Also drops platelets, but consumes red cells too: you would expect anemia and schistocytes, and there are none.
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
Correct. An ISOLATED thrombocytopenia — red cells and white cells untouched — with a normal smear after a viral illness. The absence of schistocytes is what separates it from the microangiopathies.
Aplastic anemia
Would take all three lines down, and here hemoglobin and white cells are normal.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Consumes platelets alongside clotting factors, with schistocytes and deranged coagulation studies rather than an isolated fall.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, platelets

cbc.io: e — Discuss the clinical significance of abnormalities in red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
cbc.q: A 44-year-old woman has confusion, fever and bruising. Her results are platelets 22,000/µL (150,000–400,000) · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL (12.0–15.5) · reticulocyte count 6.4% (0.5–2.5) · smear numerous schistocytes (—). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
Drops platelets alone and leaves the smear normal; there would be no anemia and no fragmented cells.
Iron deficiency anemia
Microcytic and hypo-proliferative, with a raised rather than reduced platelet count and no schistocytes.
A thrombotic microangiopathy
Correct. Low platelets PLUS a hemolytic anemia with schistocytes is consumption inside small vessels — red cells are being sheared as they pass. The fever and confusion complete the classic pentad.
Hereditary spherocytosis
Produces round cells without central pallor, not fragments, and does not consume platelets.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, schistocytes

cbc.io: a — Explain the components of a complete blood count
cbc.q: A 58-year-old man has headaches, itching after hot showers and a ruddy face. He does not smoke. His results are hemoglobin 19.8 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · hematocrit 59% (41–53) · white blood cell count 14,200/µL (4,500–11,000) · platelets 612,000/µL (150,000–400,000). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Polycythemia vera

Correct. All THREE lines are raised, which points at a clonal marrow disorder rather than a response to anything. A secondary cause drives red cells alone; it has no reason to raise white cells and platelets too.
Chronic hypoxia from lung disease
Raises red cells only, as an appropriate erythropoietin response. It leaves white cells and platelets alone.
Dehydration
Concentrates everything proportionally and resolves with fluids; it does not produce a platelet count of 612,000.
Anemia of chronic disease
The wrong direction entirely — that lowers hemoglobin rather than raising it.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, red cell count raised

cbc.io: g — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns associated with microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anemia
cbc.q: A 47-year-old man with cirrhosis has a routine panel. His results are hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · mean corpuscular volume 103 fL (80–100) · smear cells with a dark centre inside the pale area (—) · vitamin B12 and folate normal (—). What is the most likely cause?
opts: Vitamin B12 deficiency has impaired DNA synthesis
B12 is normal, and megaloblastic change gives macroovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils rather than targets.
Iron is being lost chronically from the gut
Iron deficiency is microcytic; this volume is 103 fL, which is the wrong direction.
The spleen is sequestering red cells
Hypersplenism lowers counts but does not create the target appearance; redundant membrane does.
Liver disease has added redundant membrane to the red cells

Correct. Those are target cells — a bullseye produced by too much membrane for the volume of hemoglobin. Liver disease and splenectomy are the two classic causes, and the macrocytosis here is non-megaloblastic.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, target cells

cbc.io: e — Discuss the clinical significance of abnormalities in red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
cbc.q: A 66-year-old man has anemia and a firm enlarged spleen. His results are hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · smear teardrop-shaped red cells (—) · platelets 96,000/µL (150,000–400,000) · white blood cell count 3,800/µL (4,500–11,000). What is the most likely cause?
opts: The spleen has been removed
The spleen is present and enlarged, and asplenia gives Howell-Jolly bodies and target cells rather than teardrops.
Oxidant stress is denaturing hemoglobin
That gives Heinz bodies and bite cells, and needs a supravital stain to demonstrate.
The marrow is being infiltrated and replaced
Correct. Teardrop cells are made when red cells squeeze out of a marrow packed with scar tissue or tumour. With cytopenias in all three lines and splenomegaly, infiltration is the mechanism.
Iron stores are exhausted
Iron deficiency is microcytic and hypochromic and does not produce teardrop forms or pancytopenia.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, teardrop cells

cbc.io: b — Explain the difference between hemoglobin and hematocrit
cbc.q: A results screen shows a value that does not look right to the clinician. The results are hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · hematocrit 48% (41–53). Why is this pair implausible?
opts: The hematocrit should equal the hemoglobin
They measure different things — an amount in a volume against a percentage of packed cells — so they are never equal.
The hemoglobin should be roughly three times the hematocrit
The multiplication runs the other way; this would predict a hematocrit of 3 from a hemoglobin of 9.
Both values are normal, so nothing is wrong
The hemoglobin is well below its range, so the panel is not normal even before the mismatch is considered.
The hematocrit should be roughly three times the hemoglobin
Correct. Multiply the hemoglobin by three and the hematocrit should land nearby — 9 predicts about 27, not 48. A pair that far apart means a sampling or analyser problem worth repeating.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, hemoglobin against hematocrit

cbc.io: c — Discuss red blood cell indices
cbc.q: A panel reports the indices below. The results are mean corpuscular volume 74 fL (80–100) · mean corpuscular hemoglobin 23 pg (27–33) · mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration 29 g/dL (32–36). How are these cells best described?
opts: Macrocytic and normochromic
Macrocytic would need a volume above 100; this is 74, at the other end.
Normocytic and hyperchromic
The volume is not normal, and hyperchromic would need the concentration ABOVE 36 rather than below 32.
Microcytic and hypochromic
Correct. Volume below range makes them small, and both hemoglobin indices below range make them pale — central pallor exceeding a third of the diameter. Iron deficiency and thalassemia sit here.
Microcytic and hyperchromic
The size is right but the colour is not — a concentration of 29 is below the range, so the cells are pale, not dense.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, red cell indices

cbc.io: h — Compare and contrast laboratory tests used in the evaluation of anemia
cbc.q: A 55-year-old woman has a microcytic anemia. Her results are mean corpuscular volume 76 fL (80–100) · ferritin 120 ng/mL (15–200) · serum iron 82 µg/dL (60–170) · total iron-binding capacity 310 µg/dL (250–400) · smear no stippling (—). What does this pattern point to?
opts: Iron deficiency anemia
Every iron study is normal, which is precisely what iron deficiency cannot look like.
Lead poisoning
The other cause of microcytosis with normal iron — but it is excluded here by the absence of basophilic stippling.
Anemia of chronic disease
Ferritin would be raised and binding capacity reduced; both sit mid-range.
Thalassemia trait
Correct. Microcytic with all three iron studies normal and no stippling — the algorithm's endpoint. Iron is available, so the small cells are a production defect rather than a supply problem.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, microcytic algorithm

cbc.io: e — Discuss the clinical significance of abnormalities in red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
cbc.q: A 62-year-old woman on prednisone for polymyalgia has a raised white count and feels well, with no fever. Her results are white blood cell count 14,600/µL (4,500–11,000) · neutrophils 82% (54–62) · bands 2% (0–5) · eosinophils 0% (1–3). What is the most likely cause?
opts: An occult bacterial infection
Would come with a left shift; bands are normal at 2% and the patient has no fever.
Corticosteroids have demarginated neutrophils

Correct. Steroids detach neutrophils from the vessel wall into the circulating pool, so the count rises without any new production — which is why bands stay normal. They also suppress eosinophils, and here eosinophils are zero.
A myeloproliferative disorder
Would usually disturb more than one line and persist; this is explained by an obvious drug.
An allergic reaction
Raises eosinophils. They are absent here, which points the opposite way.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, demargination

cbc.io: e — Discuss the clinical significance of abnormalities in red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
cbc.q: A 39-year-old woman with heavy periods has these results hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL (12.0–15.5) · mean corpuscular volume 71 fL (80–100) · platelets 580,000/µL (150,000–400,000) · ferritin 7 ng/mL (15–200). How should the platelet count be read?
opts: Evidence of a second, independent bone marrow disorder
Unnecessary. The anemia already explains it, and invoking two diagnoses where one accounts for both findings is the error being tested.
A reactive rise that iron deficiency itself causes

Correct. Iron deficiency is one of the listed causes of a raised platelet count, alongside trauma, acute hemorrhage and polycythemia vera. It needs no separate workup — treat the iron deficiency and it settles.
A laboratory artefact requiring a repeat sample
There is nothing inconsistent here — the value fits the clinical picture rather than contradicting it.
A sign of impending bleeding
A high platelet count is not a bleeding risk in this setting; her bleeding is menstrual and is the cause, not the consequence.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, platelets raised

cbc.io: e — Discuss the clinical significance of abnormalities in red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
cbc.q: A 71-year-old man has back pain and anemia. His results are hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · smear red cells stacked in chains like rows of coins (—) · total protein 10.8 g/dL (6.0–8.3) · erythrocyte sedimentation rate 112 mm/hr (0–20). What is the most likely cause?
opts: Antibodies are agglutinating the red cells
Agglutination clumps cells irregularly rather than stacking them in neat chains, and it is temperature-dependent.
The marrow is infiltrated by fibrous tissue
That gives teardrop cells, not rouleaux, and would not raise the total protein.
Raised serum proteins have neutralised the cells' surface charge

Correct. That stacking is rouleaux: red cells normally repel each other with a negative surface charge, and excess protein cancels it so they clump in chains. The very high total protein and sedimentation rate fit a paraprotein.
The cells have lost membrane and become spherical
Spherocytes are round and individual; they do not stack, and the hemoglobin concentration index would rise.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, rouleaux

cbc.io: a — Explain the components of a complete blood count
cbc.q: A well 30-year-old man has a pre-employment panel. His results are hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · mean corpuscular volume 91 fL (80–100) · white blood cell count 7,600/µL (4,500–11,000) · platelets 268,000/µL (150,000–400,000). How should this panel be reported?
opts: Normal, with no further testing indicated

Correct. Every value sits inside its range. Recognising a normal panel is a real skill — a reference range is the mean plus or minus two standard deviations, so chasing values that are merely near an edge generates work rather than answers.
Early iron deficiency, because the volume is below the midpoint
Being below the middle of a range is not being outside it. 91 fL is unambiguously normal.
Mild anemia, because the hemoglobin is not at the top of the range
Anemia means falling below the lower limit, not below the maximum. 15.1 is comfortably inside.
Thrombocytopenia, because the platelet count is under 300,000
The lower limit is 150,000, so 268,000 sits comfortably inside the range. Thrombocytopenia means falling below the floor, not below the midpoint.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, reference ranges

cbc.io: h — Compare and contrast laboratory tests used in the evaluation of anemia
cbc.q: A 63-year-old man is found to have iron deficiency anemia on a routine panel. He reports no bleeding. His results are hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL (13.5–17.5) · mean corpuscular volume 70 fL (80–100) · ferritin 5 ng/mL (15–200). What must accompany treatment?
opts: Nothing beyond oral iron and a repeat panel
This is the trap. The anemia will correct and the cause will be missed, which is the outcome the teaching exists to prevent.
Bone marrow biopsy
Not indicated for straightforward iron deficiency, where the mechanism is loss rather than a production failure.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis
That investigates thalassemia, and thalassemia does not lower ferritin to 5.
Evaluation for occult blood loss

Correct. In a man of this age iron deficiency is a bleeding diagnosis until proven otherwise, and it is often the first sign of gastrointestinal bleeding. Replacing the iron without finding the leak treats the number, not the patient.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, iron deficiency

cbc.io: e — Discuss the clinical significance of abnormalities in red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
cbc.q: A 60-year-old man has fatigue and early satiety with a very large spleen. His results are white blood cell count 96,000/µL (4,500–11,000) · differential the full range of maturing granulocytes (—) · platelets 540,000/µL (150,000–400,000) · hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL (13.5–17.5). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A myeloproliferative disorder

Correct. A white count near 100,000 with granulocytes at every stage of maturation and a massive spleen is clonal overproduction, not a response to infection. The raised platelets and mild anemia fit the same process.
A bacterial infection
Even severe sepsis rarely reaches 96,000, and it produces mature neutrophils with bands rather than the entire maturation series.
A viral infection
Raises lymphocytes and does not produce granulocytes at every stage or splenomegaly of this degree.
Corticosteroid therapy
Demargination can raise the count, but only modestly, and it does not enlarge the spleen or raise platelets.
cbc.cite: Complete Blood Count and Hematology Diagnostics - Shahsv.pptx, white cell count raised

chem.io: e — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns seen in renal, hepatic and metabolic disorders
chem.q: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting and deep rapid breathing. Her results are glucose 512 mg/dL (70–99) · bicarbonate 8 mEq/L (22–29) · sodium 132 mEq/L (135–145) · chloride 96 mEq/L (98–107) · urine ketones large (negative). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Diabetic ketoacidosis

Correct. High glucose, low bicarbonate and ketones, with an anion gap of 132 − (96 + 8) = 28 against a normal of 8 to 12. The unmeasured acids are the ketones, and the deep rapid breathing is respiratory compensation.
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
Glucose is usually far higher and, decisively, there is little or no ketosis and no acidosis — bicarbonate would be near normal.
Lactic acidosis
Also widens the gap, but it does not produce large urine ketones or a glucose of 512.
Diarrhoeal bicarbonate loss
Lowers bicarbonate too, but as a NORMAL gap acidosis with a raised chloride — here the gap is wide at 28.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, anion gap and metabolic pattern

chem.io: e — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns seen in renal, hepatic and metabolic disorders
chem.q: An 82-year-old man has had three days of vomiting and poor intake. He is hypotensive. His results are blood urea nitrogen 62 mg/dL (7–20) · creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (0.6–1.2) · sodium 148 mEq/L (135–145) · urine specific gravity 1.032 (1.005–1.030). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Intrinsic renal failure
Would give a ratio below 20 to 1, because damaged tubules stop reabsorbing urea preferentially, and the urine would be inappropriately dilute.
Postrenal obstruction
Can raise both, but there is no obstructive history and the picture here is one of volume depletion.
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
Causes a LOW sodium with concentrated urine; the sodium here is high at 148.
Prerenal azotemia

Correct. The urea to creatinine ratio is about 39 to 1, well above 20 to 1, which places the problem BEFORE the kidney — poor perfusion. The concentrated urine confirms the tubules are working hard to retain water.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, urea to creatinine ratio

chem.io: e — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns seen in renal, hepatic and metabolic disorders
chem.q: A 58-year-old woman is oliguric after several days of an aminoglycoside. Her results are blood urea nitrogen 48 mg/dL (7–20) · creatinine 4.2 mg/dL (0.6–1.2) · potassium 5.9 mEq/L (3.5–5.0) · bicarbonate 17 mEq/L (22–29). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Prerenal azotemia
Would need a ratio above 20 to 1. Here urea has risen much less than creatinine, which is the opposite pattern.
Intrinsic renal failure

Correct. The ratio is about 11 to 1 — below 20 to 1 — so the damage is in the kidney itself, and the drug is the obvious insult. The high potassium and low bicarbonate are the expected consequences of failing excretion.
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Bicarbonate is low, but there is no hyperglycaemia and no ketosis, and creatinine would not reach 4.2 from that alone.
Diabetes insipidus
Produces water loss and a high sodium with dilute urine, not a rising creatinine and hyperkalaemia.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, urea to creatinine ratio

chem.io: i — Explain laboratory evaluation of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis
chem.q: A 24-year-old woman has had a week of vomiting from hyperemesis. Her results are sodium 131 mEq/L (135–145) · potassium 2.9 mEq/L (3.5–5.0) · chloride 88 mEq/L (98–107) · bicarbonate 36 mEq/L (22–29). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Bicarbonate would be low rather than 36, and glucose and ketones would be raised.
Diarrhoeal bicarbonate loss
Lowers bicarbonate and raises chloride — the mirror image of this panel.
Metabolic alkalosis from protracted vomiting

Correct. Sodium, potassium and chloride all down with bicarbonate UP is the vomiting panel. It persists because volume, potassium and chloride depletion force the kidney to keep reabsorbing bicarbonate — which is why it does not correct until chloride and potassium are replaced.
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
Lowers sodium, but leaves potassium, chloride and bicarbonate largely alone.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, the vomiting case

chem.io: i — Explain laboratory evaluation of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis
chem.q: A 68-year-old man with small cell lung cancer is confused. He looks euvolaemic. His results are sodium 118 mEq/L (135–145) · serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg (275–295) · urine osmolality 580 mOsm/kg (—) · urine sodium 62 mEq/L (—). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone

Correct. A genuinely low serum osmolality with inappropriately CONCENTRATED urine — the kidney should be making dilute urine to shed water and is doing the opposite. Small cell lung cancer is a classic source.
Pseudohyponatraemia
There the measured sodium is low but serum osmolality is NORMAL, because the sodium is diluted by lipid or protein rather than by water. Here osmolality is genuinely low.
Diabetes insipidus
The opposite defect — too little antidiuretic effect, giving a high sodium and dilute urine.
Prerenal azotemia from volume depletion
He is euvolaemic, and urea and creatinine are not the abnormality here.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, fluid balance

chem.io: i — Explain laboratory evaluation of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis
chem.q: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes has these results sodium 128 mEq/L (135–145) · glucose 700 mg/dL (70–99) · serum osmolality 300 mOsm/kg (275–295). How should the sodium be interpreted?
opts: It is diluted by the glucose and corrects once that is treated

Correct. Glucose pulls water into the vascular space, lowering measured sodium by roughly 1.6 to 2 mEq/L for every 100 mg/dL above normal — about 10 here. The osmolality is HIGH, which tells you the patient is not water-overloaded at all.
It represents true water excess needing fluid restriction
True hypotonic hyponatraemia comes with a LOW osmolality. This one is raised at 300, so restricting fluid would be the wrong move.
It is a laboratory artefact from lipaemic serum
That is pseudohyponatraemia, and it leaves osmolality normal rather than raised. The glucose here explains it.
It indicates the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
That gives a low serum osmolality with concentrated urine; neither applies.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, three pitfalls

chem.io: e — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns seen in renal, hepatic and metabolic disorders
chem.q: A 34-year-old woman has malaise and dark urine for a week. Her results are aspartate aminotransferase 1,840 units/L (10–40) · alanine aminotransferase 2,210 units/L (7–56) · alkaline phosphatase 128 units/L (44–147) · total bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL (0.2–1.2). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Alcoholic hepatitis
Rarely pushes transaminases past a few hundred, and the ratio runs the other way — aspartate above alanine, classically more than two to one.
Acute viral hepatitis

Correct. Transaminases in the THOUSANDS have only three causes — viral, ischaemic and toxic — and the alkaline phosphatase is barely moved, making this hepatocellular rather than cholestatic. Alanine exceeding aspartate fits a viral picture.
Common bile duct obstruction
Would raise alkaline phosphatase out of proportion; here it is inside its range.
Chronic hepatitis C
Gives mild persistent elevations, not values in the thousands with acute jaundice.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, hepatic patterns

chem.io: e — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns seen in renal, hepatic and metabolic disorders
chem.q: A 61-year-old woman has painless jaundice and pale stools. Her results are alkaline phosphatase 612 units/L (44–147) · gamma-glutamyl transferase 488 units/L (9–48) · alanine aminotransferase 74 units/L (7–56) · total bilirubin 9.4 mg/dL (0.2–1.2). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute viral hepatitis
Hepatocellular — transaminases would dominate, in the hundreds or thousands, with alkaline phosphatase comparatively spared.
A cholestatic process obstructing bile flow

Correct. Alkaline phosphatase raised far out of proportion to the transaminases is the cholestatic signature, and the high gamma-glutamyl transferase confirms the alkaline phosphatase is hepatic rather than bone.
Paget disease of bone
Also raises alkaline phosphatase, but from bone: the gamma-glutamyl transferase would be normal and there would be no jaundice.
Alcoholic hepatitis
Gives a hepatocellular pattern with aspartate above alanine, not an isolated alkaline phosphatase of 612.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, cholestatic pattern

chem.io: e — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns seen in renal, hepatic and metabolic disorders
chem.q: A 49-year-old man who drinks heavily has tender hepatomegaly. His results are aspartate aminotransferase 186 units/L (10–40) · alanine aminotransferase 72 units/L (7–56) · alkaline phosphatase 132 units/L (44–147) · mean corpuscular volume 104 fL (80–100). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute viral hepatitis
Alanine would exceed aspartate and both would be far higher — hundreds to thousands rather than under 200.
Biliary obstruction
Alkaline phosphatase is normal here, so bile flow is not the problem.
Acetaminophen toxicity
Produces transaminases in the thousands, not a two-to-one ratio at this level.
Alcoholic liver disease

Correct. Aspartate above alanine by more than two to one is the alcohol ratio, the magnitude is modest rather than in the thousands, and the macrocytosis alongside it is the same story from the blood count.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, AST to ALT ratio

chem.io: c — Discuss basic liver function studies included in chemistry testing
chem.q: A 57-year-old man with known cirrhosis is assessed. His results are albumin 2.4 g/dL (3.5–5.0) · international normalised ratio 2.1 (0.9–1.1) · alanine aminotransferase 48 units/L (7–56) · total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL (0.2–1.2). What do these results show?
opts: Impaired synthetic function rather than active injury

Correct. Albumin and clotting factors are MADE by the liver, so a low albumin and a prolonged clotting time measure how well it works. The near-normal transaminases show little ongoing hepatocyte injury — function and injury are separate axes.
Severe acute hepatocellular injury
The transaminases mark injury and they are essentially normal. This panel is about capacity, not damage.
Biliary obstruction
Would raise alkaline phosphatase; it is not even reported as abnormal here.
Dehydration concentrating the samples
Would raise albumin rather than lower it, and would not prolong the clotting time.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, injury against function

chem.io: f — Explain the relationship between electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base disorders
chem.q: A 31-year-old man has had five days of watery diarrhoea. His results are sodium 138 mEq/L (135–145) · chloride 116 mEq/L (98–107) · bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (22–29) · potassium 3.1 mEq/L (3.5–5.0). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A high anion gap metabolic acidosis
The gap calculates to 8. A raised gap would mean unmeasured acids, and the raised chloride tells you the opposite has happened.
Metabolic alkalosis
Bicarbonate is 14, well below the range, so base has been lost rather than gained — this is an acidosis, and alkalosis would show the opposite.
A normal anion gap metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss

Correct. The gap is 138 − (116 + 14) = 8, which is normal, so no unmeasured acid has appeared — bicarbonate has simply been lost from the gut and chloride has risen to keep electrical neutrality. Hence hyperchloraemic.
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Would widen the gap and raise glucose and ketones; the chloride would not climb to 116.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, normal gap acidosis

chem.io: f — Explain the relationship between electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base disorders
chem.q: A patient's panel returns with these results sodium 140 mEq/L (135–145) · chloride 98 mEq/L (98–107) · bicarbonate 12 mEq/L (22–29). Calculate the anion gap and say what it means.
opts: 30 — a normal gap, meaning bicarbonate loss
The arithmetic is right, the interpretation is not: normal is 8 to 12, so 30 is markedly raised.
30 — a raised gap, meaning unmeasured acids
Correct. 140 − (98 + 12) = 30, against a normal of 8 to 12. A gap this wide means acid has been added rather than bicarbonate lost, and the MUDPILES list is where you go next.
12 — a normal gap, meaning bicarbonate loss
This subtracts only the chloride and forgets the bicarbonate; both anions belong in the bracket.
42 — a raised gap, meaning unmeasured acids
This adds the anions to the sodium instead of subtracting them. The conclusion is right by accident, the number is not.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, anion gap

chem.io: d — Interpret abnormal chemistry values and their clinical significance
chem.q: A 66-year-old woman on a potassium-sparing diuretic and an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor has muscle weakness. Her results are potassium 6.8 mEq/L (3.5–5.0) · creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (0.6–1.2) · bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (22–29) · electrocardiogram peaked T waves (—). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypokalaemia from diuretic use
The wrong direction — this diuretic spares potassium rather than wasting it, and the value is high.
Metabolic alkalosis driving potassium into cells
Alkalosis drives potassium IN and lowers the serum level; here bicarbonate is low, and acidosis drives potassium out.
Hyperkalaemia requiring urgent treatment

Correct. Potassium is excreted by the kidney with essentially no reabsorption, so reduced clearance plus two drugs that block its excretion is a common route to this. Small serum changes have large physiological effects, and the peaked T waves prove the membrane is already affected.
A laboratory artefact from haemolysed sample
Possible in principle, but the electrocardiogram changes show the potassium is real and acting on the heart.
chem.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, potassium

chem.io: a — Describe the urinalysis parameters: specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, ketones, leukocyte esterase, nitrites
chem.q: A 24-year-old woman has dysuria, frequency and urgency. Her urine dipstick shows leukocyte esterase positive (negative) · nitrites positive (negative) · blood trace (negative) · protein trace (negative or trace). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Urinary tract infection

Correct. Leukocyte esterase positive means pyuria — white cells are present — and a positive nitrite means bacteria have been converting urinary nitrates for more than four hours. Together with the symptoms that is an infection.
Glomerulonephritis
Would show much heavier blood and protein with red cell casts on microscopy, not trace amounts with a positive nitrite.
Rhabdomyolysis
Gives a strongly positive blood pad with no red cells on microscopy, and does not turn the nitrite pad positive.
Diabetes mellitus
Would show glucose and possibly ketones; neither is present, and it does not cause pyuria.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, the two infection pads

chem.io: a — Describe the urinalysis parameters: specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, ketones, leukocyte esterase, nitrites
chem.q: A 30-year-old woman has clear dysuria and frequency. Her dipstick shows leukocyte esterase positive (negative) · nitrites NEGATIVE (negative) · blood trace (negative). How should the negative nitrite be read?
opts: It excludes bacterial infection, so no culture is needed
This is the trap. A positive nitrite is helpful; a negative one is not, because the test misses about half of infections.
It means the sample was contaminated
Contamination is suggested by squamous epithelial cells on microscopy, not by a negative nitrite.
It does not exclude infection, and culture should still be sent

Correct. Nitrite sensitivity is only about 50%, and the commonest organism is rarely a nitrite producer, so a negative pad is weak evidence. With symptoms and a positive leukocyte esterase, send culture and sensitivity.
It means the infection is fungal rather than bacterial
Not a conclusion the pad supports — plenty of bacterial infections are nitrite negative.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, nitrite sensitivity

chem.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations
chem.q: A 12-year-old has cola-coloured urine and puffy eyes two weeks after a sore throat. His urinalysis shows blood large (negative) · protein 2+ (negative or trace) · microscopy dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts (—) · blood pressure 148/92 (—). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Glomerulonephritis

Correct. Blood AND protein together, with red cell casts, localises the bleeding to the glomerulus — casts form in the tubule, so the cells came from above it. The preceding pharyngitis and hypertension complete the picture.
Urinary tract infection
Would show leukocyte esterase and nitrites, and produces neither red cell casts nor this degree of proteinuria.
Nephrolithiasis
Causes bleeding from the tract and colicky pain, but not casts, heavy protein or hypertension.
Rhabdomyolysis
The blood pad would be positive with NO red cells at all on microscopy, and there would be no casts of this type.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, blood and protein

chem.io: b — Differentiate between hematuria, hemoglobinuria and myoglobinuria
chem.q: A 26-year-old man is found after a long period immobile on the floor. His urine is dark. Results are urine blood large (negative) · urine microscopy no red blood cells seen (0–2 per field) · creatine phosphokinase 48,000 units/L (30–200) · potassium 6.1 mEq/L (3.5–5.0). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Haematuria from a kidney stone
Intact red cells would be visible on microscopy, and a stone does not raise creatine phosphokinase to 48,000.
Haemoglobinuria from intravascular haemolysis
The other pigment that fits a pad-positive, cell-negative result — but that is confirmed by a raised unconjugated bilirubin, not by muscle enzymes.
Myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis

Correct. The pad detects heme, so it cannot tell red cells, free haemoglobin and myoglobin apart. A strongly positive pad with NO red cells means one of the latter two, and the creatine phosphokinase names it as muscle.
Urinary tract infection
Would show leukocyte esterase and nitrites and would not explain the enzyme level or the hyperkalaemia.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, the three meanings of blood

chem.io: b — Differentiate between hematuria, hemoglobinuria and myoglobinuria
chem.q: A 34-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has dark urine and jaundice. Results are urine blood large (negative) · urine microscopy no red blood cells seen (0–2 per field) · unconjugated bilirubin 5.2 mg/dL (0.2–0.8) · creatine phosphokinase 112 units/L (30–200). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis
Would show a markedly raised creatine phosphokinase; it is normal at 112.
Haemoglobinuria from intravascular haemolysis

Correct. Pad positive with no red cells again — but here the muscle enzyme is normal and the unconjugated bilirubin is high, which is a direct product of haemoglobin breakdown. That is the confirming test for this pigment.
Haematuria from glomerulonephritis
Intact red cells and casts would appear on microscopy, and neither is present.
Bilirubinuria from biliary obstruction
Obstruction raises CONJUGATED bilirubin, which is the water-soluble form that appears in urine; here the raised fraction is unconjugated.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, haemoglobinuria

chem.io: a — Describe the urinalysis parameters: specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, ketones, leukocyte esterase, nitrites
chem.q: A 22-year-old woman has lost weight and feels unwell. Her dipstick shows ketones large (negative) · glucose 3+ (negative) · specific gravity 1.028 (1.005–1.030) · protein negative (negative or trace). What is the immediate next step?
opts: Send urine culture and sensitivity
Nothing here suggests infection — leukocyte esterase and nitrites are not raised.
Arrange a twenty-four hour urine collection
That is the follow-up for proteinuria, and protein is negative.
Check the blood glucose

Correct. Ketones mean cells are burning fatty acids instead of glucose, and the stated next move is always to check the blood sugar. With glucose also spilling into the urine, uncontrolled diabetes is the working diagnosis until that number comes back.
Repeat the dipstick in two weeks
Delay is unsafe when ketones are large and glucose is spilling; this needs a number today.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, ketones and glucose

chem.io: a — Describe the urinalysis parameters: specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, ketones, leukocyte esterase, nitrites
chem.q: A 27-year-old pregnant woman has a routine dipstick. Results are glucose trace (negative) · blood glucose 84 mg/dL (70–99) · protein trace (negative or trace) · ketones negative (negative). What best explains the glucose in the urine?
opts: Pregnancy lowers the tubular reabsorption threshold

Correct. Glucose is filtered then wholly reabsorbed proximally until the blood level exceeds the tubular threshold, around 180 mg/dL. With a normal blood glucose, glucose in the urine means the threshold itself has fallen — and in pregnancy a trace is expected.
The blood glucose must have been high earlier in the day
Possible in principle, but pregnancy is the specific, common explanation being tested, and a trace is a recognised normal finding.
The sample is contaminated
Contamination introduces squamous cells and bacteria, not glucose.
This is early diabetic ketoacidosis
Ketones are negative and the blood glucose is normal; neither fits.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, tubular threshold

chem.io: a — Describe the urinalysis parameters: specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, ketones, leukocyte esterase, nitrites
chem.q: A 71-year-old man has bone pain and anaemia. His dipstick shows protein negative (negative or trace) · total serum protein 11.2 g/dL (6.0–8.3) · albumin 3.1 g/dL (3.5–5.0) · smear rouleaux (—). Why is the dipstick protein negative, and what should be ordered?
opts: The kidney is undamaged, so no further urine testing is needed
The dipstick has a known blind spot here; treating its silence as reassurance is exactly the trap.
Repeat the dipstick on a first morning sample
Concentrating the sample does not fix a test that cannot detect the molecule in question.
Send a twenty-four hour collection for total protein
Quantifies protein but does not identify light chains; electrophoresis is what characterises them.
Strips miss Bence Jones protein — send urine protein electrophoresis

Correct. Reagent strips detect albumin and are insensitive to the light chains of a paraprotein, so a negative pad does not exclude them. With rouleaux and a total protein of 11.2, electrophoresis is the test that finds them.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, the myeloma trap

chem.io: a — Describe the urinalysis parameters: specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, ketones, leukocyte esterase, nitrites
chem.q: A patient has a computed tomography study with intravenous contrast, and a urinalysis is sent afterwards. Results are specific gravity 1.048 (1.005–1.030) · protein negative (negative or trace) · glucose negative (negative) · blood negative (negative). What best explains the specific gravity?
opts: Radiographic contrast, whose large particles inflate the reading

Correct. Specific gravity weighs solutes against water, so particle SIZE matters as well as number — marbles against glitter. Contrast has unusually large molecules and characteristically drives the value above 1.040.
Severe dehydration
Concentrates urine, but rarely past about 1.035, and the recent contrast is the specific explanation here.
Diabetes insipidus
Produces the opposite — dilute urine with a LOW specific gravity.
Heavy proteinuria adding solute
Protein is negative on this sample, so it is contributing nothing.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, specific gravity

chem.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations
chem.q: A 44-year-old man passes large volumes of pale urine and is constantly thirsty. Results are urine specific gravity 1.002 (1.005–1.030) · serum sodium 149 mEq/L (135–145) · glucose 92 mg/dL (70–99) · urine glucose negative (negative). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Diabetes mellitus with osmotic diuresis
Would show glucose in the blood and the urine; both are normal here.
Diabetes insipidus

Correct. Dilute urine while the serum sodium is HIGH is the giveaway — the kidney is shedding water it should be keeping, so antidiuretic effect is missing or unheard. Normal glucose rules out the osmotic alternative.
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
The mirror image of this: too MUCH antidiuretic effect, so the sodium falls and the urine is inappropriately concentrated rather than dilute.
Psychogenic polydipsia
Also gives dilute urine, but from drinking too much, so the serum sodium would be low or normal rather than 149.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, specific gravity low

chem.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations
chem.q: A 39-year-old woman has recurrent infections with a urea-splitting organism. Results are urine pH 8.2 (4.5–8.0) · nitrites positive (negative) · leukocyte esterase positive (negative) · microscopy coffin-lid crystals (—). What kind of stone is she forming, and what is the treatment principle?
opts: Uric acid — alkalinise the urine
Uric acid stones form in ACIDIC urine and are treated by alkalinising it; this urine is already alkaline at 8.2.
Struvite — treat the infection

Correct. Alkaline urine is produced by urease-producing bacteria splitting urea to ammonia, and struvite and triple phosphate stones form in that environment. The stone is a consequence of the infection, so the infection is the target.
Calcium oxalate — restrict dietary oxalate
The other acidic-urine stone. It is the commonest overall but does not fit an alkaline pH with urease-producing organisms.
Cystine — increase fluid intake alone
A rare hereditary stone that is not driven by infection or by an alkaline pH.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, pH and stones

chem.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations
chem.q: A patient with a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis has a urinalysis. Results are serum bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (22–29) · serum chloride 114 mEq/L (98–107) · urine pH 6.8 (4.5–8.0). What does the urine pH suggest?
opts: Appropriate renal compensation for the acidosis
Compensation would produce an acidic urine. This value shows the opposite of an appropriate response.
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Widens the anion gap; this acidosis has a normal gap and no ketones are reported.
A urea-splitting urinary infection
Would also raise urine pH, but there is no pyuria or nitrite here and it would not cause a systemic acidosis.
Renal tubular acidosis, because the kidney is failing to excrete acid

Correct. In an acidosis the urine should be maximally acidic as the kidney dumps hydrogen ions. A pH of 6.8 in that setting means it cannot — which is the name trap: renal tubular ACIDOSIS gives an inappropriately ALKALINE urine.
chem.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, renal tubular acidosis

chem.io: a — Describe the urinalysis parameters: specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, ketones, leukocyte esterase, nitrites
chem.q: A 38-year-old man has ankle swelling. His dipstick shows protein 3+ (negative or trace) · blood negative (negative) · serum albumin 2.2 g/dL (3.5–5.0) · leukocyte esterase negative (negative). What is the appropriate next test?
opts: Urine culture and sensitivity
Nothing suggests infection: leukocyte esterase is negative and there are no urinary symptoms.
Repeat the dipstick after exercise
Exercise causes transient functional proteinuria, but this patient has hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, so the finding is not benign.
A twenty-four hour urine collection to quantify the protein
Correct. The strip is semi-quantitative — trace, 1+, 2+ are graded estimates rather than measurements — so heavy proteinuria with a low albumin and oedema needs quantifying before anything else.
Serum creatine phosphokinase
That investigates myoglobinuria, and the blood pad is negative.

chem.io: a — Describe the urinalysis parameters: specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, ketones, leukocyte esterase, nitrites
chem.q: A urinalysis is reported from a mid-stream sample in a well woman. Results are microscopy more than 20 squamous epithelial cells per high power field (—) · bacteria few (—) · leukocyte esterase negative (negative) · nitrites negative (negative). How should the bacteria be interpreted?
opts: Significant bacteriuria requiring antibiotics
Bacteria count as significant when they come from a straight catheter sample, or alongside raised white cells and a positive leukocyte esterase. Neither applies.
Probably contamination, and the sample should be repeated

Correct. More than twenty squamous cells per field means the sample picked up skin and genital flora on the way out. With negative leukocyte esterase and nitrites there is no evidence of true infection.
Evidence of pyelonephritis
Would require pyuria at minimum, plus casts and systemic features; nothing here supports it.
A urea-splitting infection
Would raise the urine pH and usually turn nitrites positive; both are unremarkable.

chem.io: a — Describe the urinalysis parameters: specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, ketones, leukocyte esterase, nitrites
chem.q: A well 25-year-old man has a routine urinalysis. Results are specific gravity 1.018 (1.005–1.030) · pH 6.0 (4.5–8.0) · protein, glucose, ketones, blood, bilirubin all negative (negative) · leukocyte esterase and nitrites negative (negative). How should this be reported?
opts: Abnormal, because the specific gravity should be 1.000
A specific gravity of 1.000 would be pure water. It is expected to carry a value, and 1.018 is mid-range.
Abnormal, because the pH should be 7.0
Urine pH is normally acidic to neutral and ranges widely with diet; 6.0 is unremarkable.
Inadequate, because microscopy was not performed
Microscopy is added when the strip or the clinical picture calls for it, not routinely on a screening sample that is entirely negative.
Normal

Correct. Six pads should read negative — leukocyte esterase, nitrites, ketones, glucose, blood and bilirubin — with protein negative or trace. Specific gravity and pH are the two that always carry a value rather than being simply negative, and both sit in range.

chem.io: d — Interpret abnormal chemistry values and their clinical significance
chem.q: A 63-year-old woman with breast cancer has confusion and constipation. Her results are calcium 13.8 mg/dL (8.5–10.5) · albumin 4.1 g/dL (3.5–5.0) · creatinine 1.7 mg/dL (0.6–1.2) · phosphate 2.2 mg/dL (2.5–4.5). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pseudohypercalcaemia from a high albumin
Albumin is normal at 4.1, so there is no binding artefact to correct for.
Primary hypoparathyroidism
Parathyroid hormone raises serum calcium, so losing it lowers the calcium. This panel shows the opposite problem entirely.
Chronic kidney disease with secondary changes
Typically gives a LOW calcium with a HIGH phosphate — both the reverse of this panel.
Hypercalcaemia of malignancy

Correct. A genuinely high calcium with a normal albumin — so it is not a measurement artefact of protein binding — in someone with a known cancer. The low phosphate and rising creatinine fit, and the confusion and constipation are the classic symptoms.

chem.io: d — Interpret abnormal chemistry values and their clinical significance
chem.q: An 84-year-old woman weighing 42 kg has these results creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (0.6–1.2) · blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL (7–20) · albumin 2.8 g/dL (3.5–5.0). How should the creatinine be interpreted?
opts: It confirms normal kidney function
This is the trap the value is designed to catch — reading the number without asking who produced it.
It indicates prerenal azotemia
The ratio is about 26 to 1, which is suggestive, but the question asks about the creatinine itself and the muscle-mass caveat is the point.
It is falsely raised by her low albumin
Albumin does not affect creatinine measurement; that binding correction applies to calcium.
It may conceal reduced filtration, because she has little muscle

Correct. Creatinine comes from muscle metabolism, so an elderly or cachectic patient generates less of it and can hold a normal-looking value while filtration is genuinely impaired. A number inside the range is not the same as a normal kidney.
